lead: A staircase carries people from floor to floor, and each sloping flight is a slab that spans along the slope or across it. In the dog-legged stair, the commonest in Indian houses and offices, two flights run side by side in opposite directions with a half landing between them. Its flight is designed as an inclined one-way slab, the waist slab, after the sloping load is converted to load per metre of horizontal run. Only a few syllabi list staircases, but where they do, a full dog-legged design is a standard long question.
prereq: You need One-way slabs; the landing that spans across the stair is designed the same way.

blocks.text: The riser R is the height of one step and the tread T its horizontal width; the going is the horizontal length of a flight (number of treads × T). A comfortable step keeps 2R + T between about 550 and 700 mm; 160 mm and 300 mm give 620 mm. The waist is the thickness of the sloping slab measured at right angles to its soffit (cl. 33.3).

items: By plan shape: straight flight; quarter-turn; dog-legged (two parallel flights, no gap between them, half landing); open well (a gap or well between the flights, often round a lift); bifurcated; spiral and helical.

Spanning across (transversely): each step is a small cantilever from a wall or a central spine beam, or spans between two side walls or two stringer beams. The steps carry the load; the waist is thin.
Spanning along the slope (longitudinally): the waist slab with its steps spans between landings or beams at the top and bottom of the flight. The dog-legged stair is usually designed this way.
Tread-riser (folded plate) stairs have no waist; each tread and riser act together as a folded slab.
Supported at the top and bottom by beams parallel to the risers: span = centre-to-centre of those beams.
Spanning onto the edge of a landing slab that itself spans parallel to the risers: span = going + at each end half the landing width or 1 m, whichever is smaller.
Landing slab spanning in the same direction as the flight: the two act as one slab between the supporting beams or walls, the going measured horizontally.
Where flights or landings cross at right angles (open wells), a load on the common area may be taken half in each direction.

blocks.where: The waist of thickness t weighs 25t × √(R² + T²)/T kN per m² of plan, because the sloping slab is longer than its plan. The steps add the triangle 25 × R/2 (R in m) per m² of plan. Live load and floor finish are taken on plan.

blocks.text: The flight is then a simply supported one-way slab on its horizontal effective span: M<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> l²/8, steel along the slope in the bottom of the waist, distribution bars across, and the usual shear and deflection checks. Where the soffit has a re-entrant corner, at the top of a flight that meets a landing, a bottom bar bent round that corner would pull out through the cover when it takes tension. So the flight bars run straight on into the top of the landing and the landing bars run straight on into the flight, crossing, each with its development length.

examples.question: Design the flight of a dog-legged staircase: floor-to-floor height 3.2 m, riser 160 mm, tread 300 mm, landings 1.25 m wide at both ends spanning across the stair hall onto walls. Live load 3 kN/m², finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415, 20 mm cover, 12 mm bars.
steps: Steps: 3200/160 = 20 risers, 10 per flight; 9 treads, so the going is 9 × 0.300 = 2.7 m. 2R + T = 620 mm, comfortable.
Effective span (landings span parallel to the risers): 2.7 + 2 × smaller of (1.25/2, 1 m) = 2.7 + 2 × 0.625 = 3.95 m.
Waist: trial t = 180 mm, d = 180 − 20 − 6 = 154 mm. Slope factor = √(160² + 300²)/300 = 1.1333.

Loads per m² of plan: waist 25 × 0.180 × 1.1333 = 5.100; steps 25 × 0.160/2 = 2.00; finish 1.00; live 3.00; w = 11.100 kN/m², w<sub>u</sub> = 16.650 kN/m². (Taking the flight load over the landing ends, which weigh only 8.5 kN/m², is on the safe side.)
Steel: 4.6 M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub> b d²) = 0.3149; A<sub>st</sub> = 639 mm²/m. 12 mm bars (113.1 mm²): 1000 × 113.1/639 = 177 mm; provide 12 mm @ 170 mm c/c (665 mm²/m).
Distribution: 0.12 % × 1000 × 180 = 216 mm²/m; 8 mm @ 230 mm c/c across the flight.
Deflection: l/d = 3950/154 = 25.65; f<sub>s</sub> = 231 N/mm², factor ≈ 1.35, allowed 20 × 1.35 = 26.91. Safe. (A 160 mm waist fails: 29.48 against 24.79.)
Landings: each 1.25 m landing spans across the hall onto the walls as a one-way slab, carrying its own load plus the flight reactions of 32.88 kN/m from each flight it receives.
examples.answer: Waist 180 mm; main bars 12 mm @ 170 mm c/c along the slope (665 mm²/m) for M<sub>u</sub> = 32.47 kN·m/m; distribution 8 mm @ 230 mm c/c.

traps: Forgetting the slope factor: the waist load would be 25 × 0.180 = 4.50 instead of 5.10 kN/m², about 13 % low.
Using the sloping length as the span. The span is horizontal: here 3.95 m, not the sloping length of the going.
Applying the slope factor to the live load. Live load is given on plan and is used as it is.
Taking the steps as 25R per m² instead of the triangle 25R/2.

Bending the flight bottom bars round the re-entrant corner of the soffit at the upper landing; under tension they straighten and spall the cover. Run them straight on and cross them with the landing bars.

quiz.q: Define riser, tread, going and waist.
quiz.a: Riser: height of one step. Tread: horizontal width of a step. Going: horizontal length of a flight. Waist: thickness of the sloping slab measured normal to its soffit.

quiz.q: Name four staircase types by plan shape.
quiz.a: Straight, quarter-turn, dog-legged, open well (also bifurcated, spiral, helical).

quiz.q: How does a stair spanning transversely differ from a waist-slab stair?
quiz.a: Each step spans across the stair (or cantilevers from a wall or spine beam) and carries its own load; in a waist-slab stair the whole flight spans along the slope between landings.

quiz.q: Find the slope factor for R = 150 mm, T = 270 mm.
A flight has a going of 3.0 m and landings 1.5 m wide spanning parallel to the risers. Find the effective span.
quiz.a: Going + 2 × smaller of (0.75 m, 1 m) = 3.0 + 1.5 = 4.5 m.

quiz.q: A student multiplies the span of the worked example by the slope factor and designs for 4.48 m. What happens to M<sub>u</sub>?
quiz.a: M<sub>u</sub> rises by 1.1333² = 1.284 times, to 41.71 kN·m/m: about 28 % too much steel, and the code basis (horizontal span) is lost.

beyond: Not for the exam. Precast flights and helical stairs (which need a three-dimensional analysis with torsion) are common in larger buildings. Fire escape stairs follow fire codes for width and enclosure, and vibration under footfall can govern slender steel or precast stairs. Search for "helical staircase design" and "precast stair flight".

figure.caption: Left: the dog-legged plan, two flights side by side with a half landing. Below: one flight of ten 160 mm risers and nine 300 mm treads; it spans 3.95 m, from the middle of one 1.25 m landing to the middle of the other, so the 180 mm waist takes 32.47 kN·m per metre.
